questions.question: In an autoregressive language model over a token sequence y = (y_1, ..., y_T), what does the chain-rule factorization $p(y)$ express?
questions.choice_A: It writes $p(y)$ as $\prod_{t=1}^{T} p(y_t \mid y_{<t})$, turning joint sequence modeling into a series of next-token predictions.
questions.choice_B: It decomposes $p(y)$ into independent marginal probabilities $\prod_{t=1}^{T} p(y_t)$, assuming tokens are independent.
questions.choice_C: It expresses $p(y)$ as a mixture of topic distributions learned from the corpus.
questions.choice_D: It rewrites $p(y)$ as $\sum_{t=1}^{T} p(y_t \mid y_{<t})$ to avoid multiplication of small numbers.

questions.question: How is conditional language modeling $p(y \mid x)$ typically implemented in Transformer decoders for sequence-to-sequence tasks?
questions.choice_A: By decoding y first and then retrospectively conditioning on x with attention.
questions.choice_B: By providing x as part of the model’s input context (e.g., via encoder-decoder attention or prepending x) while using causal masking so targets cannot see future y tokens.
questions.choice_C: By training two independent language models, one for x and one for y, and multiplying their probabilities.
questions.choice_D: By computing $p(x \mid y)$ and inverting it using Bayes’ rule at inference time.

questions.question: Why are subword tokenization methods (e.g., BPE, WordPiece, unigram LM) generally preferred over word-level tokenization for language modeling?
questions.choice_A: They guarantee lower perplexity regardless of model or data.
questions.choice_B: They eliminate the need for special tokens such as <BOS> and <EOS>.
questions.choice_C: They reduce out-of-vocabulary issues and balance vocabulary size with the ability to compose rare words from smaller units.
questions.choice_D: They make attention computation asymptotically faster by shortening every sequence.

questions.question: What is the role of the <EOS> (end-of-sequence) token in computing the probability of a generated sequence?
questions.choice_A: It is ignored during training but used only for decoding heuristics.
questions.choice_B: It enforces a maximum sequence length by truncating longer outputs.
questions.choice_C: It indicates padding regions to be masked from loss computation.
questions.choice_D: It lets the model assign probability to termination; the full sequence likelihood includes the probability of emitting <EOS> after the final token.

questions.question: How does averaging per-token log-likelihood instead of summing it affect comparisons across sequences of different lengths?
questions.choice_A: Averaging reduces length bias by normalizing for the number of tokens, making scores more comparable across lengths.
questions.choice_B: Averaging increases the probability mass of longer sequences.
questions.choice_C: Averaging makes likelihoods incomparable across models with the same tokenizer.
questions.choice_D: Averaging is equivalent to summing because log transforms are linear.

questions.question: In maximum likelihood training of autoregressive models with teacher forcing, which statement is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Gradients flow only through sampled discrete tokens, requiring REINFORCE.
questions.choice_B: The objective minimizes cross-entropy between data and model next-token distributions, enabling standard backpropagation through the softmax.
questions.choice_C: The objective maximizes $p(y)$ by backpropagating through entire sampled sequences at inference time.
questions.choice_D: The model is trained to predict unordered bags of tokens to reduce exposure bias.

questions.question: Which definition of perplexity is standard for language models trained with negative log-likelihood?
questions.choice_A: Perplexity is the arithmetic mean of token probabilities.
questions.choice_B: Perplexity equals the inverse of the likelihood of the full sequence.
questions.choice_C: Perplexity is $\exp\!\left(\text{average negative log-likelihood per token}\right)$, i.e., $\exp(H)$ where H is the cross-entropy.
questions.choice_D: Perplexity is the number of tokens the model can predict without error.

questions.question: What is “exposure bias” in the context of autoregressive language models?
questions.choice_A: The model’s tendency to overfit frequent tokens, ignoring rare ones.
questions.choice_B: The shift in token distributions caused by domain adaptation.
questions.choice_C: The mismatch in tokenization between training and evaluation.
questions.choice_D: The train-test mismatch where the model is trained on gold histories (teacher forcing) but must condition on its own potentially flawed predictions at inference.

questions.question: Why is a causal attention mask necessary in decoder-only Transformers used for language modeling?
questions.choice_A: It prevents a token at position t from attending to positions > t, ensuring $p(y_t \mid y_{<t})$ is respected even with full self-attention.
questions.choice_B: It reduces the number of parameters by a factor of two.
questions.choice_C: It allows bidirectional context for each token during training.
questions.choice_D: It ensures the model always emits the <EOS> token after a fixed number of steps.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of byte-level tokenization for language modeling across diverse scripts and noisy text?
questions.choice_A: It yields shorter sequences than subword tokenization for all languages.
questions.choice_B: It provides a fixed, closed vocabulary that can losslessly represent any input, avoiding OOV issues without <unk>.
questions.choice_C: It removes the need for normalization or detokenization.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees better calibration than subword methods.

questions.question: When comparing two candidate outputs of different lengths under a language model, which scoring approach best mitigates the tendency to prefer shorter strings?
questions.choice_A: Use raw product of token probabilities without logs.
questions.choice_B: Use the sum of log probabilities, which removes length bias.
questions.choice_C: Use average log probability per token (or apply an explicit length penalty) to normalize for sequence length.
questions.choice_D: Use the maximum single-token probability within the sequence.

questions.question: Which statement about scheduled sampling as a remedy for exposure bias is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: It preserves the exact MLE objective while improving search.
questions.choice_B: It is guaranteed to improve perplexity on held-out data.
questions.choice_C: It avoids the need for teacher forcing by sampling entire sequences.
questions.choice_D: It mixes model predictions into the conditioning context during training, reducing train-test mismatch but breaking the unbiased MLE objective.

questions.question: What is the main effect of label smoothing during MLE training of language models?
questions.choice_A: It reduces overconfidence by distributing some probability mass to non-target tokens, often improving generalization but slightly harming exact likelihood.
questions.choice_B: It eliminates the need for softmax by using one-hot targets.
questions.choice_C: It increases the model’s capacity by adding parameters to the output layer.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees better calibration without affecting perplexity.

questions.question: Why might perplexity not always correlate with human judgments of generation quality in conditional generation tasks?
questions.choice_A: Because perplexity is computed only on the source inputs x, not on the outputs y.
questions.choice_B: Because likelihood captures how well the model fits the data distribution, while human judgments depend on decoding strategies, task goals, and pragmatic qualities not fully reflected by token-level likelihood.
questions.choice_C: Because higher perplexity always implies better diversity, which humans prefer.
questions.choice_D: Because perplexity is invariant to tokenization and thus ignores content.

questions.question: Which training property distinguishes MLE for next-token prediction from reinforcement learning objectives for sequence-level rewards?
questions.choice_A: MLE requires sampling entire sequences from the model during training.
questions.choice_B: MLE is non-differentiable and uses policy gradients.
questions.choice_C: MLE uses teacher-forced targets and standard backpropagation through differentiable softmax predictions, without the high-variance gradient estimators needed in RL.
questions.choice_D: MLE optimizes a reward defined only at the end of the sequence.

questions.question: What is a principal architectural benefit of encoder-decoder models for $p(y \mid x)$ compared to simply concatenating x and y in a decoder-only model?
questions.choice_A: They eliminate the need for positional encodings.
questions.choice_B: They can see future y tokens during training without leakage.
questions.choice_C: They train faster because they avoid attention entirely.
questions.choice_D: They provide a bidirectional representation of x via the encoder while maintaining causal decoding for y, improving conditioning without violating autoregressive constraints.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <BOS> (beginning-of-sequence) token in autoregressive training?
questions.choice_A: It provides a fixed starting context so the model can learn to predict the first token as $p(y_1 \mid \text{<BOS>})$ and subsequently shift targets by one position.
questions.choice_B: It forces the model to generate longer sequences.
questions.choice_C: It marks padding regions to be ignored by attention.
questions.choice_D: It ensures the model predicts tokens in reverse order.

questions.question: How can researchers make evaluation more comparable across models that use different tokenizers (e.g., subword vs byte-level)?
questions.choice_A: Always decode to words and compute word-level accuracy.
questions.choice_B: Report bits-per-character or normalize cross-entropy by a common unit so the metric is less sensitive to tokenization granularity.
questions.choice_C: Use only raw sequence likelihood, which is tokenization-invariant.
questions.choice_D: Ensure every model uses the same vocabulary size regardless of language.

questions.question: In beam search for conditional generation, why is a length penalty often applied to the beam scores?
questions.choice_A: To encourage the model to use rarer vocabulary items.
questions.choice_B: To match the prior distribution over lengths imposed by the dataset.
questions.choice_C: To counteract the tendency of log-likelihood sums to favor shorter outputs, improving fairness among hypotheses of different lengths.
questions.choice_D: To ensure every hypothesis ends with <EOS> at the same time step.

questions.question: From an information-theoretic perspective, which divergence does maximum likelihood estimation minimize when fitting a model $p_\theta$ to the data distribution $p_{\text{data}}$?
questions.choice_A: $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \parallel p_{\text{data}})$, encouraging mode-seeking behavior.
questions.choice_B: Jensen-Shannon divergence, encouraging balanced mode coverage.
questions.choice_C: Total variation distance, encouraging strict support matching.
questions.choice_D: $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}} \parallel p_\theta)$, encouraging mode-covering behavior consistent with assigning probability where data appears.
